utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is called, just a few administrative matters. Firstly and briefly, pre-trial brief due in respect of Croatia/Bosnia. The Chamber knows that there is a limit of 50 pages unless extension is granted. The Chamber will recall that in Kosovo, we stuck to 50 pages and didn't seek any extension. For Croatia/Bosnia, I would ask that the Rule be interpreted so that we may have 50 pages per indictment, if that's acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second point is a matter of information and so that we don't lose sight of it. The Chamber recalls that the Rule 68 reports that we file come with identification of the parameters we are applying to fulfil to the best our ability and in a reasonable way the 68 duty. It seems prudent fairly soon for us to review the parameters, in light of the cross-examination of the accused, to make sure that they don't need revision, and so I will serve a report again comparatively soon but with that objective in mind. And it may be helpful for us to have that in mind as cross-examination is developing. Third point which comes in two parts is both a general and a specific. As the Chamber knows, the accused has told us that he has a room full of the material we've served on him and which he does not turn to. The Chamber will also know that, as of the end of last week, the accused has sought, via the Registry, from us witness statements of witnesses who are about to be called, and we have made those available through the Registry to him. Now, in due course, there's going to be a very great deal of material served in respect of the Croatia/Bosnia indictment in accordance with the Rules, and we hope that that service will be effective for the accused to prepare his defence and for him to prepare for witnesses when they come. And we hope that it will not be necessary for us then to have to serve everything according to a different routine, and we would ask the Chamber not to make any decision today but, in due course, to perhaps raise the matter with the accused, because if he wants disclosure on a different basis that is more helpful to him in his work and preparation, then that can be done, but it doesn't seem to us entirely desirable that things should be being disclosed once to no effect and then on an entirely different basis. That brings me to the immediate problem -- I'm probably speaking too fast and I apologise. That brings me to the immediate problem. Next week, it is intended to call the first expert, Patrick Ball, and a witness, Lord Ashdown, whose material will cover not only Kosovo but will cover part of matters relevant to the Croatia/Bosnia indictment. One can't, I think, respectfully -- respectably expect the witness to come twice; he can only come once. So that the accused is now on notice that those are the two witnesses, or two of the major witnesses for next week. So far as Patrick Ball is concerned, the accused has had the report for months and he has notice that we intended to call him at this time for months as well. Technically, I think in terms of filing his report with the Chamber, we may be four days short of the required 30-day limit for service, and so we would seek relief in respect of that. But what we are more concerned to do is to ensure that the accused has the material or can find the material that he may need to look at to deal with that witness, because this is not just, obviously, a witness who's coming to give an account of something happened in a village. It's material he'll need to look at. What I am in a position to do, by immediately after the break, is to serve or to make available to the accused a schedule that sets out where he may find, according to the dates of the service, all the material that relate to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't we simply ensure that he has, towards the end of this week, the material? If need be, the Chamber will do it, or if you want, perhaps you could do it yourself. I think it would be much easier for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll deal with that. And the same will apply with Lord Ashdown as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So I'll simply serve his material again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient to do it at the end of the week so he can look at it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'll get it to him as soon as may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us know when you're going to serve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, of course, is not an expert; he's merely another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But as far as the expert is concerned, we have the report and that can very largely stand as the evidence in chief. Do you want to ask the witness any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should probably want him to summarise the effect of his evidence, but it may not be necessary to go into it in any great detail other than that. But as a matter of public record, it would be important to get him to deal with it to that extent. There's another expert, again whose reports have been available for months and in respect of whom the accused has had notice for months that he was to be called, Ridelmayer, R-I-D-E-L-M-A-Y-E-R. His report was filed on the 28th of February, and accordingly, depending on whether we call him next week - I think unlikely, or the week after more probable - there will be some short service in respect of which we would seek relief. But again, no prejudice to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think as far as Mr. Ridelmayer is concerned, not next week, but the week after would be better, because we've only just got the report ourselves. But we will allow short services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then, finally, the Prosecution's paper on the scope of cross-examination will be with you by, I hope, the middle of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me deal with some practical matters. We will hear the argument on Rule 92 bis on the statements, the written statements, that is, and their admissibility, on Thursday afternoon at a convenient time. There will be no need for anybody to repeat what's already in the documents which have been served, so I hope it can be relatively quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Thursday afternoon I think we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not here. Quite right. Thursday morning it will have to be. Yes, we're sitting 9.00 to 1.45 from today onwards. Yes. In that connection, the accused asked us to consider the position about 5.00 sittings, and we have done so. And in the light of his representations and in the light of various other consideration and the difficulties of sitting late for members of the staff and others, we have reconsidered that, and the result is this: that we won't sit until 5.00. We will decide on a daily basis whether it's necessary to sit beyond the normal time of 4.00 or so to 4.30 on a particular day, and we shall not sit today beyond 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the first witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Romano will call this first witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Hasan Pruthi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration. Yes, if you'd read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, can you please state your full name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Hasan Pruthi.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You were born in Gjakove on the 10th of October, 1947? You are married, with three children?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm born on 10th of June [sic] -- of April [sic], 1947, father of three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think I have a problem with the translation. It's June or April?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: October. I was born in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Pruthi, you were born in October of 1947?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You're a lawyer and you're currently working as a legal advisor for the Norwegian Council of Refugees?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you worked as a judge, first in the Municipal Court of Gjakove from 1976 to 1978, and after, in Gjakove Business Court from 1978 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What's your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were most of the people in Gjakove Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were there Serbs in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were a few Serbs in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where Gjakove is located, Mr. Pruthi?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Gjakove is in -- is in the southern part of Kosova. It's between Peja and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you have any military training or experience?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I merely completed my military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I completed military service in 1973 to 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, during all the time that you worked as a lawyer and as a judge in Kosovo, more specifically in Gjakove, did you notice any difference in treatment between Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Of course I noticed a difference. I might say that in 1991, the Serbian parliament at that time made a discriminatory decision according to which the Commercial Court of Gjakove district was dissolved and about 40 employees were left on the streets without work.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, why you say that this decision was a discriminatory decision?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Because this court was an adjudicating court, and this decision was taken at a time when the Federal Ministry of Yugoslavia had given -- had greatly praised the work of this court, and there was no reason to dissolve it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the work in the Commercial Court? What was the role of the Commercial Court?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The district Commercial Court was responsible to settle economic disputes and to register firms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were there a lot of applications by Albanians to register their firms?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were applications to register firms because this was a year when the law on enterprises came into effect. It was the time of Ante Markovic. And according to this law, people were given the opportunity to register private companies and to turn their property and to start joint enterprises with public enterprises. So this court was responsible for enforcing this law and registering various kinds of property.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how did the abolishment of this court by the Serb parliament affect the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Because this court extended its authority over the entire plane of Dukagjin. It was involved in administering the economic life of this entire part of Kosova. So the abolition of this court, it was a blow to this entire part of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, if the Albanians wanted to register their private business at that time, with the abolishment of that court, where they had to go?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: At that time, there were two courts working in Kosova. There was the Pristina economic court and the one in Gjakove which was abolished. Albanians at that time who wanted to register their court [sic] at the Economic Court in Pristina were instructed and were unable to register their firms because the officers of that court refused to register them after the Gjakove court was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Pruthi, that it was difficult for the Albanians to register their property in just one court?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, because they couldn't register these firms. At the time that I'm talking about, they couldn't register these firms at the court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: There was any particular reason why they couldn't register their firms in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: According to the rules, any refusal of an application by citizens, any registration of a company needed a written reason of any failure to register it, and the court didn't supply these but merely refused them orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Also while -- during the time that you practised law in Kosovo, was there any requirement for the trade of property?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, there was. This was a time when the Serbian parliament had introduced the law on the trading of property in -- under special circumstances, which covered the territory of Kosova, which required a special approval from the Finance Ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And this requirement was mandatory to everyone, to Albanians, Serbs, to everyone in Gjakove; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was binding on everybody, but according to the discriminatory law, it prevented the trade in property on a daily basis, and citizens could not sell their property without obtaining prior approval of this ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, what was the difference in treatment between Albanians and Serbs concerning those requirements?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The treatment was not the same, in fact, because the applications of Albanians dragged and were prolonged and were not settled for a long time, while Serbian applications were settled immediately. And a large number of Albanian applications were also refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you personally know Albanians who had problems in obtaining this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were plenty of cases -- I can't give you a name, but there were many cases in which applications were refused by this ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you able to provide a percentage between Albanians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: What kind of percentage do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many applications between -- how many Serbian applications were admitted in comparison with how many Albanian applications were denied?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: You mean by this ministry?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Serbian percentage, when I'm talking about Kosova, there were fewer applications, of course, from Kosova, from Serbs, than from Albanians. But as I said before, the Albanian applications were refused and some others were settled, but over a very long period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And all the Serbian applications were admitted?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Serbs didn't dare sell their property in Kosova as long as this law was in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: While performing your duties as a lawyer and a judge as well, what was the language used in applications and documents?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: As you know, before the overthrow of Kosova's autonomy, Albanian was an official language, but not afterwards, so that communications in the district courts were made only in Serbian. I'm talking about the municipal court in Gjakove. And applications in writing always had to be made in the Serbian language. If they were made in Albanian, they were immediately sent back and refused by the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did the Albanian population complain about that situation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Some lawyers in our municipality complained to the justice ministry, the republican one, of course, but they never received a reply, even though it was the right of the Albanians to make applications in their own language. But this right was not recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pruthi. What do you know about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The KLA was a force that appeared during the war in Kosova, a force that was -- stood by the unarmed people who were suffering, were defenceless, and they always defended the population who were in such danger from the murderous Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, you said it was a force that appeared during the war. Which war are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the criminal attacks of Serbian forces and Serbian police in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Before we get there, I wanted to ask you: Were you associated to the KLA at any time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I was not connected with the KLA at any time, and I never saw KLA troops in my city at the time when the war broke out, but it was present on the outskirts of the city. It wasn't able to enter the town at that time because of the great presence of Serbian army and police inside the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, did you support the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The activities of the KLA in protecting the population from crimes and from murders, as I said before, at the hands of the Serbian police and army, of course I supported, because its activities were in the interests of the population, who were totally defenceless at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you materialise this support in any way?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, can you briefly describe how was the life in Albania immediately before the NATO campaign?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was very tense. Life was -- it was a miserable life which can't be summarised in a few words. The people lived in tension and fear and were shut up in their homes. Only their needs for daily supplies for their families and for groceries -- one member of the family would have to go out for the market, fetch supplies, but otherwise it was impossible to go out on the streets because of the major presence of Serbian military equipment and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, when was that? Which time did you see this presence of Serbian army and police in your town?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I saw this presence from 1988, when the roads were filled with Serbian army and police vehicles who patrolled up and down the streets all day and all night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You referred to Serbian army and police. How do you know they were soldiers and police?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: You could see by their uniforms. Because the army had one uniform and the police had another, you could see who were policemen and who were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms, the police uniforms and the army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Of course; the police had a blue uniform, camouflage, while the Serbian army had green uniforms, also camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I please have the witness shown the Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, the usher will show you a series of photographs containing photographs of uniforms. Can you please take a look on those photos and see if you can identify any of the uniforms, a photo similar of the uniforms that you saw belonging to the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: For example, here's a police uniform, a Serbian police uniform here, and in this photograph up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Which number, Mr. Pruthi?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Number 6 and number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And the army?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This is the uniform of the Serbian police, number 6. And this is also a kind of uniform of the Serbian police, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you identify the uniform that the army soldiers wore at that time, looking again at the photos?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I can. Here we are. Number 9, that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned vehicles, also equipment. What kind?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about police and military vehicles of various kinds - trucks, Pinzgauers, jeeps of different kinds - and their weapons were generally automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I please have the witness shown Exhibit 17 and also, after, 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, can you look at the photos that the usher will put before you. And there are a series of photos of military and police vehicles. Can you see among them if you can identify any photo of a vehicle that you saw at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can show you. There are various vehicles in front of me which I saw at this time. I will start here. This first kind and this third kind, tanks, and this kind -- these other kinds of vehicles that I saw at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, can you please indicate the one and --

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: And the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you indicate one by one, and the usher will put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Vehicle number 7. Vehicle number 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you also indicate if you know what kind of vehicle it was and if it was a military vehicle or a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: These were both police and military vehicles. The two kinds were together. I have these kinds here in front of us in this photograph. There was also a kind of jeep that they used at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you please proceed and indicate the numbers and the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Number 2, number 15, number 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw all this equipment, all these vehicles at that time around your town, in your town. Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: You could see them on all the streets of the city, parading throughout the day, and you could hear the noise of them as they moved during the night too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You mentioned also automatic weapons. I will again ask you to look at some photos and see if you can identify any of the weapons that you saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That time, I saw the gun number 4, the gun number 1 and number 2. And there were also kinds of cannon shown, and the kind shown in photograph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So you mentioned -- the first ones you mentioned belong to sheet A, and the cannon belongs to sheet B; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, the A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. During 1998 and beginning of 1999, do you remember seeing people from other villages coming to Gjakove, coming to live in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well the flight of a part of the population from the villages roundabout Gjakove in 1998. These people streamed toward Gjakove and were pushed by Serbian police and military forces and were forced to leave their houses. These people told how they were chased by Serbian police and army, how their houses were burned, and some were killed by their fellow villagers and were always taunted by the words and were told to leave their house -- to leave their houses as soon as possible and go to Albania because what were they looking for here in Kosova? The population told how they were obliged by this horror to leave their villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you personally speak with the villagers that arrived in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I spoke to these villagers personally because we were helping to accommodate them in various houses in Gjakove at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did they tell who was pushing them away from their villages?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They showed us who was chasing them. They told us that the police and the army, the Serbian police and army, were driving them away. They had not yet left their homes when they saw their homes in fire. They saw it with their own eyes, and that they were horror-struck at the sight, and this forced them to leave their own homes and take the street of emigration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, where were you when the NATO bombing campaign started?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I was in Gjakove then, in my own home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people were you in your home?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: My own family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the members of your family?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My wife and my young daughter. When late at night we heard a shot, and then after that shot, I went out to see what was happening and then I heard the second shot coming from a hill overlooking the town called the hill of Cabrat, and then I heard the counter-fire by the Serbian forces which were deployed there. I heard different sounds of anti-aircraft fire, firing at the NATO planes flying over the city of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, did you hear or see the airplanes flying over Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what time was that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was about 9.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Was any part of the town hit by the bombing?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, it was not. They bombed the depots, the military barracks, and some other depots, military depots, which were located at Cabrat Hill. These were the two targets hit by NATO then, at that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: These two targets, they were far away from the town? They were near or they were far away from the town?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Cabrat was near my home, whereas the barracks and the depots were in the periphery of the city, in the outskirts of the city. On the next day, we found out that they were hit by NATO that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: For how long did the NATO planes fly over Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: For a short time, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you remember what time did they leave?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Maybe 15 past 9.00 or 20 past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened after the NATO airplanes left?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: They left, and then after the fire of -- anti-aircraft fire by the Serbian army, everything became calm for a couple of hours. It was at about 12.00, at midnight, when I saw a great light in the fire [as interpreted], and I was curious to see what it was. I went to the second floor of my own house to see, and across my house, in the direction of Carshia, old Carshia of the town, I saw a great fire and great smoke, accompanied by shots of all kinds, and they were found in objects, in facilities that were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How far was this old part of the town from your house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: About 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And can you describe exactly what you saw from your window?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I saw the old part of the town, Carshia e Madhe, otherwise known by this name. It was all set on fire. It has cultural, historical value, and that night it was all on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know what caused the fire?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I was informed that it was the Serbian police that set fire to this part of the town using a special substance, to all the stores of the marketplace, and they also killed some people living there, whose houses are found in this part of the town. Several people were killed, among whom well-known Doctor Izet -- in front of his own family members. Izet Hima.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How do you know that, Mr. Pruthi? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: His own family members told this. They testified to his murder to the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, where I was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did the doctor -- was he killed at the same time while the old part of the town was burning and in flames?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Dr. Hima was killed, in the most brutal manner, in front of the eyes of his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, at the time you saw the flames was a very few hours after you saw the NATO airplanes. How do you know the burning of the old centre was not a result of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The flames appeared much later than the NATO planes left. This was certain, a certain fact. There are hundreds of people who saw with their own eyes Serbian police setting fire to this old part of the town. Hundreds and hundreds of witnesses have been there. So it's a fact that everybody has been testifying to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming back to your house in your neighbourhood at that time, on the next morning you remained at home?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I used to stay at home then, and very much -- was very much worried about what was happening. On the next day, we saw Serbian police and military patrolling the streets of the town, and only some small -- some people went to some stores to buy some things they needed for their own daily living. In the evening --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Pruthi. You said police patrolling. What kind of uniform were they wearing? Were they any different from the ones you had already seen in the photos?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. They were the same uniforms I showed you in the pictures a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What exactly were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: They were just patrolling with their cars in the streets of the town, were seeing on both, you know, sides of the street what happened. They struck fear among the citizens, and nobody dared leave their homes. Everybody stayed at home after they heard what happened one night before. They were all horror-stricken and stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with your neighbours at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contacts with my neighbours then, and we were discussing together what we would do. We were counting the minutes, fearing that the worst might happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: On the second night, after the lights went out, it was about 8.00 when gunshots started, coming from automatic rifles, a lot of fire shots. We stood at home, my wife, my daughter and myself. It was around 11.00 when I heard a noise coming from the yard of my neighbour. It was a noise of, I mean, people talking. I went to the window to see what was happening. I saw a large crowd of people gathered in the yard. I opened the window to see better. Then I saw that the wall dividing my home from my neighbour, there in the yard were a large number of people. And the shots coming from the police in our street made us afraid lest that they could come to our own homes. So I went to the yard of my neighbour and joined the group of people who had gathered there and who had come from the next adjoining street, from that part of the city where the houses were on fire and from where people were driven out of their homes. They told us that they were coming from those burning homes and that they had left behind dead people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: We stayed there until before dawn, until the cars in which the Serbian police were withdrew. When the police withdrew, then we returned to our own homes. But while we were staying in that yard, I heard with my own ears the voices of police speaking and shouting, because they were close by the houses. They were telling people, "Go away. This is not your country. This is Serbia. Go to Albania," in a loud, shrieking voice. It was a sad sight to see. Then we went home to my own house with some neighbours to have some rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, was anybody hurt or injured during this time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was 6.00 in the morning. The wife of my cousin came to my house. She was crying, and she told me that her husband was killed, and she asked me to help her. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What is the name of your cousin?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: His name is Shevqet Pruthi. I rose to my feet and went with her. We went out in the street even though it was very dangerous because the streets were rife with police, Serb police. And then we went to her home, and she showed me the dead body of her husband behind the house. It was lying on the floor, on the ground. And I saw that both his soles were damaged from the fire of the automatic rifles, and part of his hand was also damaged, and his body was full of holes in the chest and in some other parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did his wife -- did his wife see what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: She didn't see what happened. This criminal deed was committed in the very eyes of his daughter. Arta is her name. She saw her father killed in front of her eyes. She saw her father die in front of her eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, did you leave your house again?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: After we buried my cousin, I returned home, and then with my wife, we were discussing what to do since we felt that we were in jeopardy staying in my neighbourhood since about 17 people had got killed that night. So we were wondering what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Is there any problem with translation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Together with my wife and my daughter, we went to my sister's, who lives in another neighbourhood in the vicinity of my neighbourhood, and we took shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: For how long did you -- first, where is your sister's house located? How far was it from your house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: My sister's house is located in the neighbourhood called Qerim, about 200 metres away from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in your sister's house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: In my sister's house, we stayed from the 26th of March up to 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people were with you in your sister's house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: My brother, my youngest brother; and the members of my sister's family. For some time, my second brother stayed there, but then he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: During the time you stayed there, what did you see happening in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: During all this time, from 8.00 fire shots started. First the light went out and then automatic shots started. It was the sign that the Serbian police began its operations in various neighbourhoods of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, did you see who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I didn't see who did the shooting, but on the 1st of April, when the Serbian police came to a neighbour, neighbour of my sister, to the house of the neighbour nearby my sister's home, they threw some substance in the two upper floors of my -- of his house, and then I saw the flames engulfing all the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How do you know -- during the time, you said you heard shooting. How do you know it was the Serbian police or army?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Usually the fire shots were heard every night, but the 1st of April is a night I will never forget in my whole life. It was the most terrible night. The police surrounded, encircled all the neighbourhood and started to kill and set fire to the houses. We changed our place. We went to some other neighbours, but there was no other place we could go because we were surrounded by the police. So we found shelter in one of the houses of the neighbourhood where there were many other people, about -- over 100, who came from other parts of the neighbourhood that -- whose houses were set fire to. So they found shelter in this very house that I am talking about. Since we were close by to the street, I saw fire brigade coming, driving by, going to the houses on fire. Then on the next day, I found out that this truck protected a house of a Serbian inhabitant not to be burnt as a result of a burning house of an Albanian citizen that was close by to this house of the Serb. This is what the witnesses told me on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Please, this night, I have to tell you that more than 20 Albanians were killed in the cellar of a house. Only a young girl managed to escape. She asked for assistance, but there was nobody to give her any assistance, and she also was burned in the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How do you know that 20 Albanians were killed? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I found out on the next day from the people who withdrew from this neighbourhood, and they had seen many people died. Apart from -- in addition to this 20 that I'm talking about, they told me that they had left many people behind because they had to flee in a hurry. They didn't have time to see what was happening, you know. And they were told to go to Albania because that was not their place, they were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did there come a time where you left again the house of your sister?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This happened on the 2nd of April when in the yard of my home, of my house, I saw many Albanians had gathered there, and together we were discussing what to do. And then we heard that we had to organise to go to Albania, because we heard the police saying on that very day when they were driving out people from their own homes to flee these houses and go to Albania. This is what they were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So did you -- did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: We left our house and went to a square. Then we lined up and found about 500 people who did not have cars. We had our own cars. And there was a bus there, the bus which couldn't take more than 60 people. So the remainder left in the direction of Qafe e Prushit border checkpoint, in the direction of Albania. It was a very sad sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you. You gathered in this square. How many people, approximately, you saw in this square?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: At that moment, I think that there were about 500 people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you see police or army at that moment at that place?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw policemen who all the time that we were staying there were keeping vigil and looking what was happening, looking at us, at our cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So what - you and the crowd of 500 people, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The people started to move in the direction of the border. Many of them were old people, women who could not walk. Some were -- were carrying their family members on carts. Some were sick. It was really a very horrible sight, very sad sight to see. And then even -- then after them, we too started to move in our cars towards the direction of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know if the police around that time do anything? Did they help the people or did they do anything?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. Nobody offered the people any help because they were in their cars and only looked at what was happening. They either patrolled or just stopped and looked at what was happening from their cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember passing any checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The first checkpoint, I remember it was about three kilometres away from the city at the place called Ura e Terzive where we were obliged to stop because the Serbian police asked us to. They asked to us hand over to them all our IDs, passports we had with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they were doing that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I remember that when I asked why the police were taking this, because I needed this document, he told me that, "There is no reason why you need it. There's no reason why you should have this document -- why you should keep this document." And then he told me not to say anything else. And then we went on to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And from Prizren, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: In Prizren, we came across a second checkpoint at which there were several policemen, and they pointed us with their hands towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you asked at any time before crossing the border to show documents?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: At the border point, when we arrived, they -- the soldiers asked us for identity documents, but of course we didn't have any because it had been taken by the police before. And they -- and we told him -- we told the soldier that all our documents had been taken by the Serbian police and we didn't have any more, and he smiled and laughed at us because he knew this, but he wanted to abuse the population. And he said that it's not true that they've taken them and, "You just don't want to hand them over." And we said, "It's true. Our documents have been taken." And then the soldiers started to take the licence plates from the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, who were at the border? You said soldiers and police. Who was asking for the documents?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: They were soldiers, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were the police present there as well?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: They didn't have police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldiers, the uniform that the soldiers were using?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was a green uniform, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Was it different or similar to the one that you have already identified?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you or the others ever receive back your documents?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When did you return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I returned on the 16th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Was your house in the same way as when you left?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Of course my house was not the same as it had been. The Serbian army had been stationed in my house for three weeks and they had destroyed everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, there were three or four families who remained there the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were they Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, they were Albanians. But also I knew from the things that the army had left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, why did you decide to leave your town and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I decided to leave the city and to leave Kosova because I saw with my own eyes people killed. I saw horror, fire. I heard from other people the most terrible stories of what they had experienced in their own homes, so I decided to leave Kosova and to save the lives of my children.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And who was causing this terror?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I believe that this terror was caused by the Serbian army and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you had lost your job when the Commercial Court in Djakovica in 1991 was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why a court is dissolved? You're a lawyer. When something like this happens, do you know why it happens?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why was the court dissolved, then?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There was no reason for the abolition of this court, because I said in my evidence, it happened when -- it happened at a time when a commission of the ministry had expressed the highest appreciation for the work of this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that decision taken by the Assembly to abolish the court, was there no reason given, or were there reasons given for this?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The reasons given at the time were not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were those reasons that were stipulated?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Assembly dissolves a court when it ascertains that it is working unlawfully, illegally?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The court worked in the most legal fashion and enforced the law in the most meticulous way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who assesses whether the court is working legally or not? You or the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The responsible authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So parliament; is that it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it only the Albanians who were employed in that court, or were there Serbs working in it too?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were a few Serbs working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the Serbs and the Albanians who lost their jobs, in fact; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Serbs had found other jobs, in time. The Serbs found other jobs before the court was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you found another job too, as far as I can read from these documents here. So there's no difference in that respect, is there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: After two years. After two years on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Albanians would apply to have their companies registered.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: On the basis of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course on the basis of the law. Did Serbs make applications to register their own companies too?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were a few applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So both the Serbs and the Albanians would make their applications to register their companies in the same place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there wasn't any discrimination there either?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about after the decision made by the Serbian parliament. I'm talking about a discriminatory decision. This was a decision which the Serbian parliament took in a way -- in an unrealistic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At all events, as a legal man yourself, I assume that you know that the law was the same for Albanians and Serbs alike.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It was not the same because it wasn't applied in the same way. The law was not applied in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what sense was it not applied?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There were cases in which the Albanian applications were turned down, and there's no point in saying it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am going back to this question precisely because -- and let me ask you a question, actually, because you're a legal man, you're a lawyer, and you must know the answer to this question. So let me start by asking you a question. You said that, quite simply, the Albanian applications were obstructed, they were placed on ice, if I can put it that way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said -- you described that when Albanians made their applications for their shops, companies, and so on, to register them, that they had to wait a long time and that there was a great deal of obstruction and that they had to wait indefinitely, that the authorities obstructed this.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: At the time I'm talking about, when I was chairman of this court, this was true, because applications were obstructed by the leaders of the Commercial Court in Pristina, that is, after the abolition of the Court in Gjakove. Albanians were obstructed and prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the obstruction consisted in the fact that the applications were kept for a long time and there was no response to them for a long time; is that it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Oral replies were given immediately and they were told that they didn't have the right to register. This happened at the Pristina court, and people who submitted applications were mistreated. A very small number did register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're a lawyer yourself, and you should know, you ought to know that on the basis of that law, if you do not receive registration in a brief period of time, it is considered that the company is registered lawfully. Do you remember provisions stating that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: If -- if applications are made to authorities, they were obliged to reply in writing and not for the application to be given back immediately into the hand of the applicant without any kind of reply. There were plenty of cases of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am saying that that is impossible following the letter of the law itself, because in the law it is stated that if there is no reply after a certain deadline, after a short period of time has elapsed, it is considered that the answer and response has been automatically allowed and that the company has been registered. This was a provision to avoid corruption, discrimination, friendly ties with officials. So I'm well aware of provisions of this kind. Is that right or is it not?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Many impossible things happened in the time I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let's clear this point up. If somebody tables an application, they can send it through the post, for example, send to the court and receives no reply from the court within the deadline prescribed by law, then that piece of paper and his application is considered to have been approved. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I claim that it is impossible --

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: They didn't act in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They didn't have to do anything, and they could not prevent you from registering your company anyway. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I can merely stress one detail. The employees of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs came several times to my office to warn me to stop registering property according to Ante Markovic's law. And on the final occasion, these people took all the registration ledgers of the court and took them to the police. This is an unprecedented act in jurisprudence, and this happened in the Gjakove Commercial Court. This was a time when people were registering firms with mixed capital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now 11.00. We'll adjourn for half an hour. Mr. Pruthi, could you remember in this adjournment and any others there may be not to speak to any one about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, at half past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that Albanians were obstructed in registering their shops, how can you explain the fact that on the 24th of March, when the war broke out on the territory of the municipality of Djakovica, there were 8.900 privately owned firms owned by Albanians and they were operating normally?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: All these firms were registered before, before this latest change that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct, but for example, from 1994, 861 gasoline stations were registered in Kosovo, that is to say, after all of this that you have said. Only 20 of them were Serb owned out of 861. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that a law was passed on special trading in immobile property. Do you know that that law pertained to the territory of all of Serbia, including Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The law on the trading of property on special circumstances, that was not included in that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Ministry of Finance had to give approval for the buying and selling of immobile property.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Article 3 of that law says the Ministry of Finance shall approve of the buying and selling of immobile property when it assesses that this does not affect the ethnic pattern of the population or the migration of the members of a certain national or ethnic group and when this buying and selling does not cause anxiety or uncertainty or inequality of right among the citizens of a different ethnic or national group.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The law was discriminatory because it did not give the right to the owners to transfer his property without prior consent of this ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have precisely been talking about the reasons for that. Since you are talking about discrimination, I should like to remind you of the following: In your municipality, there was one case. For example, in the village of Meca, in the 1980s, Miodrag Saric was killed in his field, before the eyes of his entire family, because he did not want to sell his field. Do you remember that case? At that time, you were still a judge.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This is not true. I was not a lawyer then, but this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not true that Miodrag Saric was killed in the field in the village of Meca, in the municipality of Djakovica, in the 1980s, in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what the witness says. He says it's not true. Just a moment, Mr. Pruthi. There's no need to answer. He says it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of other pressure and murders in order to force people to sell their property and leave their property behind?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember, for example, the village of Ratis, which is near you, how many families left that village - that's in your neighbourhood - and left their property because of beatings, rapes, torchings, in the 1980s? Do you remember these examples from the village of Ratis?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in relation to this right exercised by the Ministry of Finance, for which you say that it is discriminatory, the higher-instance authority that decided on this was a commission set up by parliament: Within 30 days you could lodge a complaint with the parliamentary commission. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Distinguished Judge, I think such questions are irrelevant. I am not called here to explain the procedure, I think, of the parliament or of the law, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, you must allow us to be the Judges of what's relevant and not. You have given evidence about some discriminatory matters, and the accused is entitled to ask some questions about it. Just one moment. You were asked about a commission set up by parliament. Do you remember anything like that? If you don't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Justice of Yugoslavia did set up -- assessed the work of the court, and it said that the work has worked very well, in conformity with Yugoslav laws in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware that there was, as a matter of fact, a special commission that was established in order to ascertain the misdoings of your court, and this is why this commission was established?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The commission never came to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Many irregularities were ascertained then - as a matter of fact, many forgeries, too - on the basis of which registrations were carried out. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't remember to have found out such falsifications of the documents. I remember that we have implemented the law of Markovic on the enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the overall jurisdiction of this Commercial Court as a registration court was transferred to the Court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, it was not transferred to the jurisdiction of the Prizren [as interpreted]. The Commercial Court of Pristina assumed these powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say "Prizren"; I said "Pristina." I don't know what kind of interpretation you got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about other parts of the territory of Serbia, in bigger towns than Djakovica, for example, the town of Vranje, that shops from Leskovac were -- shops from Vranje, for example, were registered at the court in Leskovac. Vranje even did not have a court of its own.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know about these things. I didn't know -- didn't have how to know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In response the Prosecutor's question as to whether Serbs were refused in terms of their requests, you said that there were far less applications by Serbs. And now my question is whether Serbs were also refused like Albanians were refused?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything in that law pertain to Albanians only?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Albanians were not allowed to sell their properties without having the consent of this ministry first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether the Serbs were allowed to sell their property without the consent of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The Serbs who lived in Kosova did not allow to sell their properties without having the approval of this ministry either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that Serbs and Albanians were in the same position. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. Because the applications of the Albanians were dragged on forever by the ministry, whereas the Serb applications, the Serbs living outside the territory of Kosova were approved immediately without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct either, but let's go on because I think that we have clarified this matter. You mentioned the law on language. Do you know that the use of language is not only regulated by law but also by the Constitution of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the Albanians who -- were deprived of their right to use the Albanian language in addressing official documents even though they had this right by law. They were obliged to present various documents to the courts or other institutions of powers -- of power in Serbo-Croatian language. That's why I said earlier that the group of lawyers in our commune, in our municipality, took a stand against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the law of the Republic of Serbia governing use of language, it says that in municipalities in which national minorities comprise the majority population, the language of the national minority concerned is equally used officially with -- along with the Serbian language throughout the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I explained earlier that this right was trampled in the most flagrant manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you know that this is what the law says quite strictly, what I quoted a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the right existed, but it was not enforced in real terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this law also applies to Bulgarians where they are the majority, for Hungarians where they are the majority, for all other national minorities on the territory in Serbia and that it is observed everywhere?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know whether that law has been respected also in other territories. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the KLA appeared during the war. Can you answer the following question: Who, then, killed so many people before the war in terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that this was done by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. This fact I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, I am not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from the 1st of January, 1998, until the war broke out, that is to say just before the war broke out, the terrorists killed -- the terrorists killed 186 citizens who were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many households from the municipality of Djakovica were expelled at that time due to ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: What families, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serb families. I'm going to read out a number of them to you. Perhaps you will remember at least some of these families from your municipality, because you were a judge there. Babovic Miloje, then Milinko Babovic, Bogoslav Babovic, Branko Jekic, Milun Fatic [phoen], Zoran Fatic, Mika Vulic [phoen], Damjan Garic, Bogoslav Garic, Hodzoma Slovic [phoen], Radila Kicevic [phoen], Jelica Jukic, Miljic Stijovic [phoen], Slobodan Vuksanovic, Ranko Vukadinovic, Petrosav Vuksanovic, Dragutin Frentic [phoen], Nusko Stejanovic [phoen], Predrag Micunovic, Aleksandra Stojanovic, Spasoj Petkovic [phoen], Dragan Petkovic, Fron Gagovic [phoen], Vejo Ibrahimovic [phoen], Vojin Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. The witness should be allowed to answer. Mr. Pruthi, do you recognise any of those names? Can you help us about any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know these names, but I didn't keep any evidence of migration from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you lived in that town. You probably know some of these people. You probably know that they were forced out of there. Are you trying to say that you do not know any one of these people, any one of these cases?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't remember these people migrating because they were forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me remind you of some of the other names. Perhaps you knew them, and I did not read those names out. Do any of these names mean something to you? The families, I'm reading the heads of families. Milorad Radovanovic, Karovic Vujadin, Delovic Petar, Delovic Nikola, Delovic Anica, Srenev Bozidar [phoen], Jevtovic Dusan, Sarenac Roza, Bibercic Draga, Bibercic Marija, Sarovic Mara, Kovacevic Bozidar, Grubisic Nediljka [phoen], Krstic Mirko, Arandzelovac Zoran, Babovic Slobodan, Babovic Savka, Vulevic Savka, Soskic Misko, Vulevic Radan, Vulevic Vujicka [phoen], Mitic Slavko [phoen], Adzic Boris, Lakic Bosko, Dzakovic Blagoje, Simonovic Drago, Zindivic Rajko [phoen], Pantic Ljubica, Radojcic Nikola, Pantic Dragoljub, Pantic Dragomir, Pantic Momcilo, Tun Kasnjeti --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause. Again, do you know any of these names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know any of them. I said before that I didn't keep any evidence of these things, and I don't know these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Court thinks it would be pointless to read out any more names. You can put them into evidence in due course, but it's no point asking this witness about them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a list of 80 families here that were expelled. The former president of the court, and lawyer, does not know of a single case, and all of them are from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shall move on to the next question, because you talked about the situation in the municipality in response to the Prosecutor's questions related to tensions in the municipality, along with the explanation that these tensions were generated by the Serb police from 1980 onwards. Do you know of killings in the territory of the municipality of Djakovica from the beginning of 1998 until the outbreak of the war on the 24th of March, 1999, for example, the policemen that were killed: On the 1st of August, 1998, Zeljko Bozic, policeman; on the 10th of August, 1998, Zoran Jovanovic. Do you know of any one of them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of Sasa Jovanovic, policeman, on the 14th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. I know only of some citizens of Gjakove who were killed and were found in the morning on the outskirts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of a policeman on the 29th of January, 1999? The policeman was called Predrag Rakovic.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of the policeman Nebojsa Savic on the 5th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of Zoran Slavkovic, also a policeman, on the 8th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Slavoljub Stanisavljevic, also on the 8th of March, 1999? Do you know of the killing of these policemen?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know about the killing of Albanians, Albanian civilians, in the territory of Djakovica from the beginning of 1998 until the 24th of March, 1999? Pajak Binak, killed on the 4th of May, 1998? Do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of the killing of Nisa Nedjar [phoen] on the 19th of May, 1998? The 19th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of the killing of Abaz Hoti on the 18th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of Krasniqi Prec on the 6th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Krasniqi Prend? They were both killed on the same day. And Merturi Mira and Merturi Prend?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All four on the same day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of the killing of Dreni Zef on the 29th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That happened in Djakovica. What about Kelmendi Haxhi, on the 24th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the 24th of January, 1999, when Kelmendi Besim and Kelmendi Shaban and Kurti Samir were killed, as well as Kurti Hisin [phoen]. You don't remember this big killing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he doesn't. Mr. Milosevic, I don't really think there's much point going on putting more names to him when he doesn't remember. You can deal with this, Mr. Pruthi. Do you know any more details of those who you say were killed and their bodies were found on the outskirts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I am asking questions with respect to the killings of Albanians in the Djakovica municipality, and Djakovica is not an overly large town, and every citizen of that municipality must have known about these killings; not one of them, but many of them. There are a large number of them here that I have quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've made your point. There's no point repeating it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't go on quoting and enumerating because it is obvious that the witness knows nothing about a single killing that was committed by the KLA up until the beginning of the war. But as there were many of these killings, the question arises as to who made the problem: the terrorist killers or the policemen who were protecting citizens from those terrorists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, would you like to comment on that Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 1480 to 1489. assertion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who was doing the killing before the war, as far as you were aware? If you can assist us, tell us; if you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you like to be a little more specific in the question that you just put? It was: "Who made the problem: the terrorist killers or the policemen who were protecting citizens from those terrorists?" Perhaps you'd like to specify more clearly what you mean by "the problem."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used the word that was used by the witness, namely, that it was the police who made problems. And as I presented an enormous list of killings which the KLA terrorists committed, precisely on the territory of Djakovica municipality up until the start of the war, I wanted to hear from the witness how he assesses the situation. Who actually caused all this?
