Was it really the police or was it the terrorists who had killed so many people, and, for the most part, civilians, as you can see, and amongst them, a large number of Albanians, too, as you can see. Let me remind you that 196 Albanians were killed by the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have clarified it, Mr. Milosevic. You have clarified it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I just wish to draw your attention to the fact that there's been an inversion here. That's the key word, "inversion." Inversion the red thread going through all these testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in Djakovica when the bombing started and that from the hills, the army shot at the planes. Do you remember whether any part of the town was hit that particular night?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I saw the anti-aircraft firing from the hill of Cabrat when they fired on the NATO aircraft with shells of various colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that particular night the barracks was hit and that around the barracks was a densely populated area with many Albanian houses and that several projectiles which missed the barracks hit those houses? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The depots and the military barracks are alongside the river, and it is not an inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that next to the places targeted by NATO planes, there were no houses belonging to citizens; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: There are in the slightly upper portion. There were no houses in the area around the depot and the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me be more precise and specific in asking my questions. Did NATO planes hit any houses in Djakovica? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No. No NATO aircraft hit any house. I can say so with a full sense of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me remind you that I have even shown photographs here of the facilities that were hit in Djakovica, objects that were hit, and they were not depots or warehouses of any kind. You claim that after the bombing, the police went out onto the streets to set fire to houses and not to put the fires out, to extinguish the fires. Is that what you're saying? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It's ridiculous to use the word "putting out fires" or "extinguishing fires." They went out to start fires - and there are an enormous number of witnesses who saw this with their own eyes - setting fire to the old market area and killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the bombing caused a number of houses to be set on fire, but do you know that the majority of the citizens in those houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. The witness has said that no houses were hit by the bombing. Are you suggesting, Mr. Milosevic, that the bombing in fact set houses on fire? If so, the witness should be asked if that is true or not, if he agrees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I'm saying, and I should like to add that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will ask -- let us ask the witness what his recollection of it is. Were any houses set on fire by the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bombing caused no fires in houses of the city of Gjakove, not a single house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Everybody knows this. All the citizens of Gjakove know this. It's a well-known truth. Not a single bomb from a single NATO aircraft ever fell on a roof of a house in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you later on how many bombs were dropped on Djakovica, but I should like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pointless going on with this witness. He says not. Now, if you've got contrary evidence, you can adduce it in due course, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them you saw here, but yes, I can move on. I wish to establish one more fact. Everything that the witness said here, he used the word that he had heard, and not that he had seen. He kept saying he had heard the police setting fire to, he had heard that the police had killed somebody, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With my own eyes, I saw two policemen setting fire to a house, the measure [as interpreted] of my sister's neighbours. I saw this for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that particular night, the night in question when NATO bombed the Djakovica territory, was there street fighting between the KLA members and the army and police?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I didn't see this. I don't know about this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the police shot when 500 of you had been gathered there. Who did the police shoot at? You said that they didn't shoot at you, so who did the police shoot at? Was it only the police who were doing the shooting or anybody else? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: People saw the police with their own eyes, firing at Albanian civilians. Twenty people were killed and burnt in the cellar of a house, and dozens of others in the same neighbourhood. This was related by residents of the city on the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why do you usually take shelter in a basement or cellar when there's a bombing on or some other danger threatening?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Because of fear of the police. Because we felt safer in the cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the 500 of you who had collected in front of your house, you didn't go -- take to the cellars because you feared the police?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: When I said 500 people, I meant when we got together to go to Albania, driven out of our homes by the Serb police. This is when I mentioned the number 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention the fact that anybody had been expelling you or that anybody had even knocked on the front doors of your houses. You didn't mention any of that.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I think that the Serb atrocities, the murder of my first cousin, whom I saw with my own eyes, the state to which his body was reduced lying behind his home, as well as other atrocities that people kept recounting were the reasons why we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have a piece of information that a cousin of yours died in the clashes between the police and the KLA. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That is ridiculous, very ridiculous. This is not at all true. His daughter saw her father being killed with her own eyes. He was shot in front of her eyes in the most atrocious manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who killed people in the most atrocious manner or generally in a terrible manner in Kosovo and Metohija? Do you know who did that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a very general question. Perhaps you can ask something a bit more particular.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May we take it that all the victims that are left after a NATO attack and the clashes between the army and police on one side and the KLA on the other, you would ascribe all that to the police force, to the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. And I base it on facts given by the eyewitnesses to these crimes and atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, in answer to questions from the other side, that you didn't see who was knocking but that it was certainly the Serb police. That was your conclusion. How do you know who was shooting? Shooting, not knocking. Shooting. Who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The police were in front of my own door. I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you see -- Mr. Pruthi, help us with this: Did you see the police shooting at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When do you think? When are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the period between the NATO bombing and your leaving Djakovica, did you see the police shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see police shooting with my own eyes, but others saw them shooting, who experienced those moments and who recounted those to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea at all as to who in Djakovica killed during the war -- here I have a list of 11 policemen. The ones I read out earlier on was before the war, but who killed 11 policemen in Djakovica during the war? That's what I'm asking you now. Do you have any idea? That means from the 20 --

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this. I have no knowledge of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that I have a list here of 61 members of the army who were killed on the territory of Djakovica municipality between the 24th of March up until the end of the war? From the 24th of March up until the end of the war, 61 soldiers. Do you have any idea who killed them? Were they killed by the soldiers, the police, and the army too?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm not aware of how they got killed. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that you saw fire brigades but that they just went to put out the fire on one Serb house.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know where the fire truck was going and what purpose it had, but on the next day, the people who came from that area told us that the fire truck was there to protect the Serb houses lest the fire from the Albanian house spread there too. This was testified to by several witnesses who saw it with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that nobody offered any assistance to the citizens of Djakovica and that the police just stood by and watched. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They didn't offer any assistance to the Albanian population. On the contrary, they just -- all of them just escorted them and mistreated them in the most brutal way on their way to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention any brutal way in which they mistreated them. Could you tell me what was this mistreatment, this brutal way that they treated them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I think I was clear when I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that you were travelling towards the border. You did not explain that anybody mistreated you on your way to the border.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Don't you think it's an act of mistreatment when Serbian police, when we arrived at the first roadblock, in the most harsh way mistreated the citizens in their cars, asking them to hand over their IDs, ridiculing them, and showing them the place where they were to go from where they would never return to Kosova they told them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were mistreating them by asking for their IDs. Is that what the police did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's just said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there was tension in Djakovica with the police presence, and I read out the names of the many people who were killed and you didn't remember a single one, Albanians or Serbs. Do you know the Ymer Grezda Street in Djakovica and number 134A in particular where, two days prior to the bombing, the KLA launched an attack, executed an attack on a vehicle belonging to the police patrol? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were members of the KLA from Albania or local ones?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that before the beginning of the war that there was a lot of tension and that life did not evolve normally. Now I'm going to ask you a concrete, specific question with respect to work and the functioning of companies in Djakovica which functioned right up until the war. As you were president of the Commercial Court, I assume that you know enough about that. The Emin Duraku company, a cotton mill which had 6.800 workers, 120 Serbs, the director was an Albanian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was a firm or factory by that name in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the Metaliku company with 800 employees, only 10 of them Serbs, the director once again an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: All these firms that you mention, as well as others, after Kosova was deprived of its autonomy, they were all destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just talking about companies which functioned until the beginning of the war, which were working up until the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I am not clear. What do you mean by that? I don't get the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean that those companies in Djakovica were functioning. They were operational even, as you say, that the Commercial Court had been dissolved and its competencies and authorities transferred to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: You are mixing up things. At the time that you are asking about, none of these firms were functioning. The enterprises you are mentioning were not operational then. They were in a deplorable situation in terms of economic state. And the Commercial Court was not in Gjakove in 1991, it was transferred, I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the court now, I'm asking about the firms. You're a lawyer, you live in Djakovica, and you're well-acquainted with the firms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that the firms were not operational. Now, can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about the motor factory, 1.200 employees, only ten of them Serbs, and the director once again was an Albanian? Electrical motor factory.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I know that this firm, the electrical motor factory, existed and that its director was an Albanian. It was a joint enterprise, joint stock enterprise, from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the model factory with 400 employees, several Serbs that you can count on the fingers of your hand, and the director once again an Albanian, producing carpentry-wear. Dolarija [phoen].

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: At the time that you are talking about, this firm, too, was not operational because it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean "destroyed"?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: In the sense of economic rentability. Because in the economy of Gjakove, the Serb parliament introduced violent measures. All of the profitable economies was subjected to violent measures; therefore, those measures had an impact on their profitability, and as such, the firm that you are talking about was also destroyed, was ruined, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Agimi slaughterhouse, 120 employees, 10 of them Serbs, the director once again an Albanian. Was that operational?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can avoid going through a very long list, can you assist us in this way, Mr. Pruthi: In the period we are talking about, namely the period leading up to the NATO bombing campaign, were any of the enterprises in Djakovica operating normally or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, none of the firms in the Gjakove municipality were operational on the eve of the war because their capital was all ruined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Tik Dukagjin, was that operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He's answered the question now, so we must move on to another topic. He says none were operational.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanians were employed in the Municipal Assembly of Djakovica? Was the Municipal Assembly operating at all?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This Assembly had technicians, technical staff of lower ranks, a small number, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Municipal Assembly, that is to say in the municipal administration in Djakovica, there were 320 Albanians employed and 210 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Isa Grezda Medical Centre in Djakovica? Was it working?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: It worked, but in very hard conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in this medical centre, Isa Grezda, there were 780 employees and 740 of them were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the exact number of this medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the heating plant worked in town? Not a single Serb was employed at the heating plant, only Albanians.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either. And do you know about the Agimi Trading Company, that is to say, the one that had retail shops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through this. Now, I think we've spent long enough on this topic. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you got anything else on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall expect you to wind this up fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't finish quickly because so many untruths have been said that I have to refute them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment. Now, you've been cross-examining for an hour and a quarter and you really should be coming to an end. The witness has dealt with the matters. You have a contrary case and you can put the contrary case to us in due course. You can put the evidence which you say supports your case before us. But there's no point going on arguing with the witness when he says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were all shops closed or were they open in Djakovica, before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Most of the shops were closed in Gjakove because people didn't dare go out. It was too dangerous. There was a very small number of shops that were open and where Serbs were employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about your assertion that Albanians were discriminated against, and I presented a series of companies here where it is quite obvious that 99 per cent or 95 per cent of all employees were Albanians and all the managers of these companies were Albanians. So your assertion now is that all of this is not true.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The truth is that the majority of the Albanian shops weren't working. Some self-service stores where Serbs were working were open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware, for example, that the bank Investbanka in Djakovica had -- all its employees were Albanians and an Albanian manager? Was that bank working?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that? Do you know that in the territory of the municipality of Djakovica, in the local police, there were 68 Albanians who were employed there at the very outset, at the very beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your own brother was the manager of the hydro system, that is to say, the water supply company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: My brother was not the manager of this company. The accused has mixed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He did not work at the hydro system, your brother?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: My brother never worked at the water supply company in Gjakove. One brother was a merchant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This area that you mentioned by the border with Albania - you mentioned it at the beginning of your testimony - that area is called Zla Reka?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I have never heard of this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Reka e Keqe, this area. Reka e Keqe, that's the area, isn't it, in Albania, from Djakovica towards the Albanian border? That's the area I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that area along the Albanian border was the recruitment centre as well as the training centre for KLA members and that's where they took their oath as well?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the organiser there was Naim Maljoku, a former JNA officer who came from Zagreb in 1998?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this area is largely populated by Albanians, migrants who came from Albania in 1945 and even more so after 1948?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. And do you know that from that area, all the major attacks were launched in 1998 in the territory of Djakovica and its outskirts?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Translate it for me again, please.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: What kind of attacks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are wasting time in this matter. The witness knows -- had said he knows nothing about this. He knows nothing about the KLA. Now, the way to deal with it is, rather than arguing with him, for you to put the evidence which you claim to have before us in due course. Now, we have to get on with this trial, and in those circumstances, you must finish your cross-examination. You've put your case very fully to the witness. You must finish in the next five minutes, and we'll move on to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can deny me the right of cross-examination altogether, but he's a judge, he's a lawyer from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All this is a matter of argument, and in those circumstances, there's no need to address us on it. Now, you've got the right to cross-examine. You use it very fully. Now, will you kindly finish this witness, because cross-examination has to be reasonable and to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war, 898 bombs were thrown on Djakovica - the area of Djakovica, that is - 898 bombs fell there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: No, I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is your assertion that not a single bomb hit a single house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: That's exactly what I say. I will say it again. Not a single bomb hit a single roof in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, the house of a Serb was demolished. His name is Nikic. It was hit by a bomb. But not only his house, but also a few Albanian houses around his was hit. Do you know about that at least?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no point in putting to the witness something which he's already dealt with. He says not a single house was hit, and that's his answer, so there's no point trying to put other matters to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm putting a specific question: Does the witness know that the centre of Djakovica was bombed, for example, when the SUP building was targeted, the police building?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This building was hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was the SUP building hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This building is on the outskirts, on the way out of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but whether it is or not, was it hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was hit. I don't know who hit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when that building was targeted, that Gjoci, an Albanian lawyer, was killed - he was in his bathroom - because he lived in the neighbourhood of that building? A colleague of yours. Do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I know that my colleague died during the war. This fact is known to me. I was in Albania, and when I returned from Albania, I was told that he died in the war, was killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A NATO bomb?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that not a single Albanian from the 18 villages of the Djakovica municipality where Albanian Catholics lived did not move out, did not leave his or her village, although the KLA made every effort to have them removed as well?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the village of Meca, where the villagers were calling the army to come to free them from KLA pressures, since they were making them leave and go to Albania? Do you know of that example?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement, you mentioned that the town was attacked from the hill of Cabrat.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, when the NATO bombing started, anti-aircraft fire started from the hill of Cabrat, and later this hill was struck by NATO forces. This is above the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip these questions since obviously they're of no use. Do you know about the village of Batusa, two kilometres away from town and also the village of Borovina that the terrorists expelled the entire village to the town of Djakovica and that the villagers returned to the village only when the army drove away the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the village of Junik where the terrorists, when they had to withdraw before the army, they took along with them 700 women and children to act as a human shield, a human shield for them until they got to the border? When they reached the border, they let them go back to Junik.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the following: that 18.000 persons left Djakovica and went to Albania?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the population of Djakovica, the municipality of Djakovica, is 110.000, whereas the population of the town of Djakovica is 70.000?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I can't -- there's no way that I can know the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of the village of Lukbunar, where the KLA forced the entire village to go to Albania and then the army returned them? All the way from Vrbnica, they returned them to the village, and when they got back to the village, the village was intact, nothing had been touched in the village. Do you know of that incident?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know about these incidents. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have only one issue to raise, Your Honour, just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know you haven't finished, but we've given you a limited time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me just put one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more. I'm going to select one of these out of all these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does the witness know that at the beginning of April, in the village of Glodjane, the KLA detained 21 Serbs and two Romany, that they tortured them and then they took them to the village of Donji Ratis and executed them by Lake Radonish? They were discovered 15 days later, buried by the Orthodox cemetery. There were children killed there. Babies were found there with bottles. 21 Serbs and two Romanies first tortured and taken to the village of Donji Ratis and then killed, executed in the canal by Lake Radonish. Do you know of that incident, at least?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. It's pointless to put any more questions anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, in your evidence in chief, you told the Court about the killing of your first nephew -- or a cousin, it was. I understand that evidence to be that you did not see the killing itself. Later on, in cross-examination, told the Court, I quote: "The murder of my first cousin whom I saw with my own eyes." Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I didn't see this murder. The murder took place in front of the eyes of his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have a couple of clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The first one is just you have just answered a question saying that you did not see the killing of your cousin. I just would like to know if you -- did you see the body?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw his body. I saw his body with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When did you see the body?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I saw the body on the morning of the 26th, when I went to the scene of the incident with my cousin's wife. And my cousin's wife said, "What shall we do?" And I said, "We must report this case to the police." And we did as I said, and we reported the incident to the police. And we expected the police to come to investigate the case, and a few hours later, the police came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: The judge --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pruthi. And just to clarify, so you saw the body on the scene where --

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: We saw the body in situ.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And can you describe how was the body? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Yes. The body was lying on the ground on its back, and I saw that the two soles of the feet were very badly injured, I believe by a volley of automatic rifle fire. And one hand was also almost detached. There were several bullet holes in the chest. And I saw that the two soles of the feet had been hit and had been damaged, almost detached, and that one palm of the hand was injured and almost cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Also --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. You can finish.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: We waited for the police, and the investigating judge and the police came a few hours later. I went out to see the investigating judge, and I was immediately surrounded by the police. And I went up to the investigating judge and met him, and immediately I was surrounded by the police. There were about 12 policemen, and they didn't allow us to move. The investigating judge asked me where the body is, and I told him that it's behind the house. "Where is the other body?" Because another neighbour of ours, Avni Ferizi, was killed that night and I told him where the house was. And the judge said, "We will go to see Avni first and then we'll come to you, to your cousin," and that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know the outcome of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: He came back from the neighbour's house, and I thought, Well, now we'll go to the scene and examine the body as according to the legal procedure. But opposite happened. It's incredible for me as a lawyer, because the judge simply said, "There's no need to investigate on the site. You can bury him." And he immediately went away and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pruthi. On cross-examination, the accused said that -- alleged that 196 Albanians were killed by the KLA. Do you have any evidence of these killings, about the fact that 196 Albanians were killed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: I have no information about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It was also alleged that the KLA ordered or pushed the villagers outside their homes. Do you also have any evidence about this fact?

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: If the KLA at any time ordered or pushed Albanian villagers outside their homes.

utterances.speaker: HASAN PRUTHI
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pruthi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until half past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Mr. Shabani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, would you give your full name to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: My name is Qamil Shabani, from Zheger village. I was born on the 14th of November, 1952. I am married and have four children: two sons and two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, sir, that you -- in March of 1999, you were a primary school teacher, but at this time you now have a different job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it also right, sir, that you are of Albanian ethnicity and of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, I understand, sir, that you performed your compulsory military service in 1978; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that was spent in Kranj, Slovenia, and you were part of an engineering unit at the time?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Kranj, in Slovenia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've just told us that you are a resident of the village of Zegra, of the municipality of -- is it Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm an inhabitant of Zheger village, Gnjilane municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And approximately how far away is Zegra from the actual town of Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Zheger village is 12 kilometres away from Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in March of 1999, sir, can you tell the Court how many inhabitants or how large a village Zegra was?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Zheger village at that time, that is, March 1999, had about 4.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And can you tell us: The majority of the inhabitants, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Most of the inhabitants are of Albanian ethnicity. The remainder, of a smaller number, are Serbian. If we consider the Albanian and the Serbian settlements or houses, it turns out that there is a total of 600 houses, of which about 70 belong to Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, in March of 1999, did there come a time when you were able to tell which of those houses belonged to the Serb inhabitants, and if so, how could you tell?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The Serb houses in Zheger village are situated in their own neighbourhoods, but there are also Albanian houses in the vicinity of the Serbian houses. They were mixed up. There were no partitions between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did there come a time in March when the Serbs did something in relation to their residences that would set them apart from the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It is a form of fascist manifestation which is -- was programmed in their heads, of the Serb citizens, that is, who wanted to take revenge against the Albanian population who undertook to organise them and to divide the Serbian houses from Albanian houses through putting some signs, some white cloths over them. I think that this was staged by certain Serbian citizens in Zheger village. I might mention Djuro Lazic, an inhabitant of Zheger who, together with some other Serbs in two places, in the houses of Srecko Lazic and another, have got together and decided to divide the houses in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just ask you, sir, what if anything they did that you could see that marked the houses of Serbs. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Before the paramilitaries came to Zheger, this happened. In the past in Zheger, there were Yugoslav army troops stationed there about ten days before the NATO airstrikes. That is, before the 24th of March, the army troops were deployed there with all their military arsenal, including tanks, armoured cars, cannons, and other equipment. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may be asked about this in a moment, Mr. Shabani, but for the moment, what you were asked was whether the Serbs marked their houses. Could you just deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They marked their houses with a white cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It resembles a fascist genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let's just stop there, if we may. I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Clerk, could the witness be shown some maps at this point. Exhibit 3, map 10, and if we could also have Exhibit 4, map 8 available to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'd like you first of all, Witness, to look at the map before it goes on the ELMO. Just have a look at that map.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you see your village of Zegra marked on Exhibit 3, map 10?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector and you will see it on the television screen in front of you, and if you could just point out to the Court with the pointer, on the map that's on the overhead, where your village is. No, not on the TV screen. That won't help us. Put it on -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You're now pointing to something that's marked as "Zegra," and that's your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And your evidence is that that was some 12 kilometres distant from Gnjilane; correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, 12 kilometres away from Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And there are some other villages marked in that general vicinity.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, the village of -- my village borders in the east with Vlastica village, inhabited by Albanians. To the north it borders Lladove village, also inhabited by Albanians, Albanians of Albanian ethnicity. In the south it borders the Haxhaj village. So these are the villages surrounding Zheger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we might get back to that in a moment. I'd like you to look at map 8 of Exhibit 4. Would you look at that first. It's got some very small printing on it so I want you to have a look at it before it goes on the ELMO. Now, do you see Zegra marked on that larger detailed map?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps that could go on the ELMO at this point, and you could use the pointer again and point out for the Court's benefit so they could see where Zegra is on this more detailed map.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're now pointing on the record to something that is marked in two names, "Zheger" and "Zegra," is that correct, about three inches down from Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs call it "Zegra." We call it "Zheger."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And the other village of Vlastica is also known --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The other village is Vlastica, which, as I said, lies east of Zheger village, whereas in the north is Lladove village. Then there is another village, Haxhaj village. Then come the Miraj, then is Jsufaj village, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you look just to the north, on a road, there's something called Donja. Does Donja have another name, sir? Is that the same as Donja Stubla or is it different?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It is a village that is situated south-west of Zheger village. It lies on a raised plateau. There is a Stubell village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you point that out on the map for us? Perhaps you did and I wasn't watching. I'd just ask you to look now and see if you see Donja Stubla. Sorry, my monitor is not --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You are now pointing to an area that is on a -- it's not white; it's sort of a shaded colour, showing that it's in the next municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. This village belongs to Viti municipality, whereas the other belongs to Gnjilane municipality. You see that there is a division there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir. Now, Mr. Shabani, I believe that you were about to tell us about what you saw, I think you said about ten days before March 24th. You were telling us about seeing the arrival of some military forces. Can you pick it up there and tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: During the time that talks were being held in Rambouillet, which did not have any marked effect, political effect, Serbia was preparing for its certain goal, Yugoslavia too, headed by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, let me just -- just stop there. What I asked you about is what you saw in your village, what happened in your village as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In our village came military forces of the regular army and the reservists, people of an older age but in uniforms, equipped with all the necessary arsenal - tanks, cannons, armoured cars - and other military equipment: mortars, machine-guns, and other weapons. They were deployed in the agriculture cooperative of our village at the entrance to the village, and part of the army was displaced at the exit of the village, in the south of the village, and occupied the house of Dermush Sejdiu. Over 90 people were stationed there, whereas the others used to patrol the streets of the village. They were either opening trenches along the river of Zheger, in Pidiq village, up to the border. This is what the army did. It came there with a certain, specific goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment, sir. I'm just going to ask you: You mentioned there was an agricultural area. Is that where they set up, or was there any other location in your village that they seemed to use as a congregation point or a headquarters or place of --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: They set up all their headquarters. Some were in the village, near the school, actually, in the school facilities, primary school facilities, whereas the army took its position at the entrance and at the exit of the village during all the time. During their stay there, they used to patrol the streets and check the citizens. They checked the citizens, observing what each and every one were doing, who was coming and going where, checking their personal IDs and documents, until the moment when the bombing by NATO started. Then the army became very angry, and the army forces that were deployed in our village, they started to fire, to shell the house of Ukshin Ukshini during the NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to stop you there and back up and fill in a few details, if I may, sir. Now, you've mentioned that they took up a position at the north entrance to the village. Prior to the arrival of these army troops, as you've called them, was there -- do you know whether or not there was a radiator factory in your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Near the agricultural cooperative, there's also the radiator factory, and this was used to accommodate the army. It was used for military purposes. No work went on in the factory at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned the home of Dermush Sejdiu. What did that home have to do with this? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This house, you can see by geographical position, it's to the south of the village, and it was used to accommodate soldiers and to store weapons and ammunition. So in this way, these forces surrounded the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, sir, you've mentioned in your evidence that both regular army and, I think you said, some older people as well, were they also in uniform?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. This army consisted of regular soldiers, with officers who had specific duties, according to their ranks, and there were also reservists, older people who had completed their military service a long time ago and now had come to join the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At this point, might the witness be shown some exhibits. Madam Clerk, I would that ask 17, 18, 21A and 21B be held available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to show you Exhibit 18 first when we get it ready, sir. On Exhibit 18, you will see a large sheet with a number of uniforms, and when you see it, I'm going to ask you to look at that before it's placed on the ELMO. And I'm going to ask you to tell the Court whether or not any of the people that arrived in your village prior to the 24th of March, the army or these older reservists, do you see any uniforms similar to what they were wearing in any of these photographs?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Number 1, uniform number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: That uniform was the most used. All the army had this kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Actually, before --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, we'll look at that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you look and see whether you see any other uniforms before we put it on the overhead? And then I'm going to ask ...

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: And this uniform number 2 is also -- was also worn by the army under certain circumstances. And also number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Which uniforms were worn by the older reservists? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The reservists mainly wore this uniform, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps this would be an appropriate time to place that on the ELMO and then you can point us, just so that we know what you're talking about when you said 1, 2, and 9. First of all, 1.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're pointing to what looks to be sort of a khaki green -- is that a camouflage uniform or is that a regular khaki green or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's green, and that's why -- that's why I mentioned it particularly. It's -- you can see some camouflage, but it wasn't used generally. It wasn't used when they were prepared for attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You say you also saw uniforms like number 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Number 2 was also present among the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And number 9.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: And number 9, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you show that, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 9, too. This was worn when they moved in among the village and when they took up positions in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, are you telling us that all three of these uniforms were present in the ten days leading up to the 24th of March in your village of Zegra?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All these uniforms were present during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'd like you to now -- you've told us that they came with all of the -- I think you said "military equipment," but that may be my way of referring to what you said. What kind of --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- military equipment do you recall seeing?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The military equipment that I saw when we were in a bus round their positions, we saw automatic rifles, machine-guns, and then mortars of the infantry, and then armoured vehicles patrolled. There were tanks, Pinzgauers, and other equipment --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: -- that they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to look at four sheets comprising Exhibit 17. On these four sheets there are, I believe, a total of 15 photographs. I'd like you to have a look at those photographs, if you would, please, and tell us whether you see any of the types of vehicles that you've just described for us depicted in these 15 photographs comprising Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. On this sheet, we have a tank, another kind of tank, and then an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: And then a personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The photographs on these sheets have numbers, so when you tell us "on this sheet," can you tell us what numbers you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph I have here, there's number 6, 7, 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And let's stop there. Number 6, what is that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This is a tank used by the army in their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What's number 7?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This is a small military truck which was used to carry soldiers, small groups of soldiers, to different positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number 8?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This is also a small open truck used to carry soldiers to their positions and during their patrols through the village of Zheger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you see vehicles like all three of these vehicles, 6, 7, and 8, in the village of Zegra in the days leading up to the March 24th?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, all these vehicles. They were all present in our village, and they moved round the village from north to the south, towards Gnjilane and Budriga, where they had their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you also mentioned, I believe, the word "Pinzgauers," and I think you mentioned APCs, which I understood to be armoured personnel carriers. Do you see any of those in any of the photographs comprising Exhibit 17?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The armoured vehicles and the Pinzgauers are on number 7. There, number 7. That's a Pinzgauer, as used by the army. And the armoured vehicle, but it -- it's armoured but it has rubber tires and equipped with weapons, it's number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And these were all present in your village and you saw them yourself, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them all myself with my own eyes, because at this time, we were able to see these soldiers in movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally, I don't want to take a lot of time, sir, but could you take a look at what's been marked as Exhibit 21A, please. You've told us that they also had automatic weapons. Do -- on Exhibit 21A there are five images of what appear to be weapons. Do these in any way -- are they similar at all to the automatic weapons that you saw, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The armoured -- automatic weapons which we saw are on sheet B, B1, B2, and then a gun with a long-distance sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your B and my B may be different. Would you just put the one you're looking at and tell me which one you're looking at. You're now holding what I believe to be Exhibit A. Is that actually marked B?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Here it's written B. Never mind. I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's fine. Then we've just got our numbers -- sorry. I'm going to go by the exhibit copy. I've just copied my numbers wrong. So you're now holding up a sheet that's marked 21B, and it seems to have some five weapons on it; is that correct? Put that --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- on the ELMO and tell us which ones you saw, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be 21A.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's what I thought, but apparently it's marked 21B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. These are number 1, number 2, and number 3, and then 4 and 5. The army possessed all these weapons at Zheger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned the 24th of March, 1999, and I think you told us that that was the date when NATO bombing started. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this day, which for the Albanian people of Kosova was a day when our hopes came true, and we hoped that we would be freed from Serbian and Slavic rule that had been imposed on Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: On this day --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened in your village on this day?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, when the NATO bombing started, the Albanian population was very cheerful, but the Serbian population were very angry, and this rage of theirs turned into retaliation against the Albanian population, and certain people had made certain preparations under directions from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, unless you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me tell you about the evidence, Mr. Shabani. What is most helpful to us, if you tell us what you saw and heard yourself rather than giving a commentary upon it. Could you just stick to what you saw and heard, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's true; I can only talk about what I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. My question, Witness, was: When the NATO bombing started, what happened to your village? In other words, you've told us about soldiers who were in and around your village prior to the 24th. Did they do something in particular? Did they go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: During the bombing, they started -- they became wilder and behaved much more savagely towards the Albanian population, and some soldiers who were stationed there in the agricultural cooperative, out of spite, started firing on Ukshin Ukshini's house, out of revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just direct your mind to a particular incident, if I may. You've told us earlier that soldiers were in the radiator factory. Did they stay there or did they go somewhere else in the village? And in the process, what happened?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The soldiers at this time, the regular army - that is, on the 24th of March - took up a position in trenches in order to defend themselves against NATO forces, and they expelled the inhabitants of four Albanian houses so that they could leave the radiator factory and move into the houses of these Albanians, houses which were near the agricultural cooperative. Meanwhile, other --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. Let me just ask some questions that I want to ask you, sir. We'll get along better if you listen to my question and answer that question rather than volunteering where you think we're going to go next, okay? Sir, you've told us about NATO bombing. Did NATO bombing occur in your village or around your village, or how do you know that NATO bombing occurred?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: There was no NATO bombing around our village, but we heard explosions from the distance, somewhere to the north, at a very great distance, but there was nothing in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So your village did not come under -- did not experience any NATO bombing on the 24th of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: That's right. It wasn't bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to the 24th of March, or on the 24th of March, are you aware of any KLA being in your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: There were no KLA forces in our village, and I never saw them and I never heard of any formation of this kind at this time. I'm talking about the village of Zheger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any skirmishes or exchange of gunfire or anything between the regular army troops you've described and any of the inhabitants, whether in uniform or in civilian clothing, in your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: No, there were no skirmishes between Serbian forces and local people, because we didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to move now, sir, to the 28th of March. I understand that it was a Muslim holiday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. This was the day of Bajram, which the inhabitants of Zheger were unable to celebrate because of the circumstances and because of the very tense situation, because of the army presence. So on the evening of that day of Bajram, to the east, where the village of Vlastica is, we heard a hail of gunfire and volleys lasting for about an hour, coming from the direction of the village of Pasjan, which is a Serbian village and where there were also soldiers and reservists. They shot at the village of Vlastica in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, before you move on, is that something that you know from personal experience or something someone else told you, or how do you know that the village of Vlastica came under gunfire from the Serb village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I know this from the noise that came and the gunfire and the heavy automatic weapons, and we heard all this from a distance, although it's not a very great distance, but we heard them from a distance. These were weapons that the army possessed, and it was they who opened fire on Vlastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn you now to the following day, the 29th of March, 1999. Did something happen in your village that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: On the 29th of March, in Zheger, additional troops came, paramilitaries, with eight buses and a minibus, with a licence plate from Nis. According to eyewitnesses who saw this -- because the position of my house was far from the point where the buses arrived, so I didn't see it, but other villagers have told me that eight buses and a minibus from Nis came to Zheger and went to the village school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Then, in the evening, that is, towards 6.00, the Serbian inhabitants of Zheger had prepared a plan to liquidate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, unless you know about this yourself -- I'm not asking you to give us a commentary on who planned what. I want you to tell us who did what.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Well, there was a murder in the house of the Tahir Tahiri, the chairman of the Democratic League of Kosovo, and they killed his brother, Shyqeri Tahiri, and at this place the family of Nasuf Tahiri was present, and Nasuf Tahiri's daughter, Nexharije, was wounded. The house of the LDK chairman was pointed out by local Serbs, and that was when the Albanian residents began to shed their blood, and they were defenceless and unarmed in their own homes. And on that night, on that terrible night, the residents of the houses round about, when they heard the gunfire, some of them fled from their houses, going from yard to yard, out of fear, lest they encounter Serbian forces who were ready to fire on anybody that they saw. So a number of Albanian villagers, on that night of the 29th of March, spent the night in the hill called Kushlevica, to shelter from the Serbian army that had begun their operation to expel the population. I was among them with my family, and we all spent the night up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. Before we get to the morning, there's a couple of details I want to fill in. Let's back up. You said that that evening, after these two individuals had been shot -- one was killed, Mr. Tahiri, and a girl was shot in the foot. You said later that evening -- I think you referred to Serb forces. Who are you now talking about? Who -- what kind of Serb forces? Was there one kind or a combination? Tell us, if you would, please, what kinds of Serb forces were in your village that night of the 29th.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It was a mixture of Serbian forces in Zheger. There was the regular army, there were paramilitaries who came, and then armed Serbian civilians with their own guns, and they all created a mixed Serbian force in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there any police in your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. The police station is in Zheger, too, and -- and they were also present in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the residents were frightened into leaving the village and that they went from yard to yard. What was it that was happening that caused the villagers to be frightened into leaving? Tell us what -- what it was that prompted them to leave.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: They were forced to leave by this crime that was committed on that night and the tortures to which people who were found on the roads were forced to submit. And there was a father and son who were beaten by Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries. And the population or some of them, in panic, went up to the hill of Kushlevica and spent the night of the 29th of March there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While these -- you've described the combined forces, Serb forces. Were they using their weapons in any way other than to shoot Tahiri and his daughter?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In the murder of Shyqeri Tahiri, this crime was committed with the use of automatic weapons, and his daughter was also wounded with an automatic weapon. And besides this, they fired in the air to scare the Albanian population and to drive them out of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to just focus you. As I understand, sir, you and your family also went up to hill called Kushlevica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you got there that evening, late that evening, are you able to say whether there were a lot of people, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. It was a large crowd of people, about 1.200. There were women and children, men; people of all kinds. It was raining. The weather was very wet. And all the population was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'm sorry that I stopped you earlier when you were about to tell us -- "early the next morning," that's where I stopped you and filled in some detail. Tell us about what happened early the next morning.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: On the next morning, on the 30th of March, a day that the Albanian people cannot forget because innocent victims also died on this day at the hands of Serbian forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just tell us what happened, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was when Ukshin Ukshini and his wife Miradije were murdered, on the morning of the 30th. At the same time, all the Serbian forces in the village started to enter the houses in turn, expelling the inhabitants, scaring them into leaving their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And where did the villagers go?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The residents of Zheger, when they were expelled under the threats of Serbian forces, some of them went to Stubell e Ulet, and from the north they went in the direction of Koresht, driven by Serbian forces, but most of them went to Stubell. But on this day, Skender Aliu was beaten, as was his brother Xhafer Aliu. These two were beaten in their own homes with rifle butts and told to leave their houses within a very short time, as was everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'll stop you there. How did you hear about the death of Ukshin Ukshini and the beatings of these other individuals? Was that told to you that day or on some subsequent time or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: No, not on that day. We found out from villagers who had houses close to Ukshin Ukshini's house and were expelled in our direction, that is, towards Stubell. As for Skender and Xhafer Aliu, they themselves came to Stubell and we saw their marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So they told you what happened, and you saw the evidence of the beatings yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: That's right. I saw it myself. I saw the evidence with my own eyes because it was on their face and other parts of their body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, sir, just so that I'm clear, earlier when I showed you the map of the -- the more detailed map, the second map I showed you, I asked you to point out Donja Stubla. You've today in your evidence referred to "Stubell." Is that the same place or a different place or have I got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Because the maps are in Serbo-Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: -- and not in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So the place that you indicated on the map to Their Honours as Donja Stubla, that's the place you're referring to where you and other villagers left the second time you were expelled from Zegra; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In Stubla village, not all the inhabitants could find shelter because there were very few available houses compared to the large number of people. So they found shelter in some tents which they put up in the mountain slopes in the vicinity of Stubla, Donja Stubla or the Upper Stubla. So the citizens or the inhabitants of Zheger, the Albanian citizens of Zheger, were in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So you and other refugees from Zegra went to Donja Stubla and you tried to find accommodation in that area. Have I got that more or less correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let's try and finish, if we can, this witness's evidence in chief this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, how long did you stay in Donja Stubla?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We stayed in Donja Stubla with my family from the 30th of March up to the 4th of May. During our stay there in Donja Stubla, many tragic events occurred in the surrounding areas, in the villages that -- bordering Stubla. I might mention the date of the 15th of April, when the village of Delekare of Viti municipality was likewise submitted to terrorist acts committed by the Serb paramilitary and military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, sir. Maybe I can summarise what I understand you're going to be saying, and that is: While you were at Donja Stubla, did a number of other villagers from other villages come to find refuge at Donja Stubla as well?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large number of people who came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And while you were there, are you able to give the Court a total, approximately, of how many refugees were gathered in the Donja Stubla area while you were there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. I might tell you that during the time I was there, when people came from surrounding villages like Lladove, Nosale, Remnik and Delekare, the figure of civilian population which came to upper Stubla - or lower Stubla, sorry - and in the surrounding areas, it might be approximately up to 20.000 inhabitants. This is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you've told us that you stayed there until the 4th of May. And during the time that you were at Donja Stubla, did some of these 20.000 people decide to leave that area?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. From the moment when the village of Delekare and Remnik were attacked, and Lladove as well, by the Serb paramilitary and military forces, the situation of food and drinking water for the citizens became critical with every passing hour, because people were living in nylon tents, which reminded you of a large concentration camp, I would say, in terms of the large number of people herded there, civilian population herded there, comprising mostly children, wives and -- women and men [as interpreted]. So given this deplorable situation, people started to spontaneously organise themselves.
